title: Refusal and the honest 'I don't know'
story:
A language model's objective is to produce a plausible continuation. That is not a criticism, it is a description, and almost everything about refusal follows from taking it literally.

Asked a question it has no basis for answering, the model is not choosing between answering and declining. It is producing the continuation that best fits the pattern of a question being answered — and the pattern of a question being answered is an answer. Fabrication is not a malfunction in that setting. It is the system doing the thing it does, in a case where the thing it does is not what anyone wanted.

Which means declining is a behaviour that has to be built, not a default that has to be protected. Nothing in the objective produces it, so if it is not engineered it will not appear, and the absence is invisible in exactly the situations where it matters.

Consider what changes between a demonstration and a deployment, because it is not the model's accuracy. In a demonstration a confident wrong answer looks like a right one — that is what confident means — and the audience has no way to tell them apart and no reason to try. In a deployment somebody relies on it. A fabricated citation in a contract review, a fabricated interaction in a clinical summary, a fabricated figure in an audit: the failure is not that the system was wrong but that it was wrong in a form indistinguishable from being right, and the person downstream had no signal to act on.

So the metric worth building the evaluation around is not how often the system answers correctly when the context supports an answer. It is how often it declines when the context does not — and that is a separate measurement, requiring a separate test set, because a suite made only of answerable questions cannot distinguish a system that knows when to stop from one that has never been asked to.

That last point is the one I would put in front of anything else here. An evaluation set consisting of questions the documents can answer measures only retrieval and phrasing. Add questions the documents cannot answer, and the same suite starts measuring something it previously could not see at all. The deliberately unanswerable cases are not an edge case in the test set; they are the part of the test set that tests the property under discussion.

The engineering divides into two places, and only one of them involves the model. Before generation, retrieval can decline on its own: when nothing retrieved resembles the question closely enough, the honest response is available without a model being consulted, which is both cheaper and more reliable than asking a generator to be humble. During generation, the instruction has to be explicit that answering beyond the supplied material is the failure rather than the fallback — and it has to be explicit because the objective pulls the other way and will keep pulling.

The cost is real and should be stated rather than discovered. A system tuned to decline when unsupported will decline some questions it could have answered, and users experience that as the product being worse. Refusals are visible and irritating; fabrications are invisible and pleasant right up until they are catastrophic. So the tuning is a choice about which failure the product would rather have, not a technical parameter with a correct value, and anyone choosing the threshold without knowing that is choosing by accident.

problem.name: Engineering the refusal
problem.shape: A system answers questions from retrieved material, and some questions have no answer in the material.
tell: the evaluation set contains only answerable questions
the system has never been observed to decline
confidence in the output does not vary with how well the context matched
failures are found by users rather than by tests
problem.move: Measure declining separately from answering, using a test set of questions the material deliberately cannot answer. Then put the first decision before the generator: if nothing retrieved is close enough, answer honestly without consulting a model, and instruct explicitly that going beyond the material is the failure.
problem.invariant: A plausible continuation is what the objective produces, so declining is a behaviour that must be added. Nothing in the system produces it by default, and its absence is invisible on answerable questions.
problem.breaks: Tuning towards refusal buys the safe failure with a visible one. The system will decline questions it could have answered, users read that as incapability, and there is no threshold that is correct in general — only a choice about which failure this product would rather have.

cost.time: a second evaluation set of deliberately unanswerable questions, which has to be built by hand and maintained alongside the first
cost.space: a retrieval confidence threshold and the plumbing to act on it before generation
cost.beats: trusting the generator's own expressions of uncertainty, which are produced by the same objective as the fabrications, and post-checking every answer against the sources, which is more thorough and costs another pass over everything

worked.problem: Why does a system that answers well in a demonstration fabricate in production, and what measurement would have caught it?
worked.reasoning:
Because nothing was ever measured that could have shown the difference, and the objective guarantees the behaviour that goes unmeasured.

Start from what the model is doing. Its objective is to produce a plausible continuation. Asked something it has no basis for, it is not choosing between answering and declining — it is producing the continuation that best fits the pattern of a question being answered, and that pattern is an answer. So fabrication is not a malfunction; it is the system doing what it does, in a case where what it does is not what was wanted. Declining is therefore a behaviour that has to be built rather than a default to be protected.

Now what changed between the demonstration and the deployment, which is not accuracy. In a demonstration a confident wrong answer looks exactly like a right one, because that is what confident means, and nobody watching has a way to tell them apart or a reason to try. In deployment somebody relies on it — a fabricated citation in a contract review, a fabricated figure in an audit — and the damage is not that the output was wrong but that it was wrong in a form indistinguishable from right, leaving the person downstream no signal to act on.

The measurement that would have caught it is the one I would lead with, because it is cheap and almost always missing. An evaluation set made of questions the material can answer measures retrieval and phrasing and nothing else. It cannot distinguish a system that knows when to stop from one that has never been asked to, because no case in it requires stopping. Add questions the material deliberately cannot answer and the same suite begins measuring the property under discussion. Those cases are not an edge of the test set; they are the part of it that tests this at all.

The engineering then divides in two, and only half of it involves the model. Before generation, retrieval can decline on its own: if nothing retrieved is close enough to the question, the honest response is available without consulting a generator, which is cheaper and more reliable than asking one to be humble about its own knowledge. During generation, the instruction has to say explicitly that answering beyond the supplied material is the failure rather than the fallback — explicitly, because the objective pulls the other way and does not stop pulling.

And the cost should be stated rather than discovered, because this is where the decision actually gets made. A system tuned to decline when unsupported will decline questions it could have answered, and users experience that as the product being worse. The asymmetry is the trap: refusals are visible and irritating, fabrications are invisible and pleasant until they are catastrophic. So the threshold is a choice about which failure the product would rather have, not a parameter with a correct value — and it is usually set by whoever is least aware of making a choice.

problem.practice: Take an evaluation set you have and count how many of its questions the underlying material cannot answer. If the answer is none, the suite has never tested refusal, and you do not currently know whether the system can decline.

beats.broke: The objective is to produce a plausible continuation, and the pattern of a question being answered is an answer — so with no basis for answering, the system fabricates, which is the objective working rather than failing.
beats.fix: Build declining as a behaviour: measure it with a test set of deliberately unanswerable questions, and let retrieval decline before a generator is consulted at all.
beats.cost: A system tuned to decline refuses things it could have answered, and users read that as incapability — so the threshold is a choice about which failure the product prefers, not a value that can be correct.

interview.q: Why does a system that answers well in a demonstration fabricate in production, and what measurement would have caught it?
interview.trap: Treating fabrication as a defect to be fixed in the model. It is what the objective produces when there is no basis for an answer, so the remedy is a behaviour to add and a measurement to run, not a bug to remove.
